entries.text: Anxiety, stress, and pressure are real—give yourself permission to feel them.
Children absorb everything when they’re little; if anxiety and silence are modeled as normal, the cycle continues.
Communication is essential; sharing what you feel helps regulate your inner world.
Emotional regulation is a skill worth working on.
Emotions aren’t good or bad—they simply are.
Gratitude isn’t something most people are taught, but it’s something everyone benefits from learning.
Humans naturally gravitate toward what feels familiar—even if that familiarity includes past trauma or unhealthy patterns.
Learn the vocabulary of your emotions; the more precise you are, the better you can understand yourself.
People often gravitate toward those who make them feel interesting—asking about others opens more doors than talking about yourself.
Repression is not the answer—unfelt emotions surface in other ways.
Ruptures and repairs are what strengthen relationships; they show whether something can be fixed and grown from.
Shame often blocks repair; it’s hard to open up when the other person doesn’t have the capacity to understand.
Talking to people and being vulnerable is important, but it can feel risky when you fear someone might use your openness against you.
The 90/10 principle: most people spend 90% of their time talking about the least important 10%; try flipping that.
The 'right people' make the world feel brighter—but the goal is to eventually feel that way within yourself too.
The first step in healing is becoming conscious of your wounds so you don’t continue gravitating toward them.
Understanding envy means turning inward—investigate what it reveals about your unmet needs.
Understanding whether an emotion is ‘above the neck’ or ‘below the neck’ helps identify its source and how to process it.
When you gravitate toward someone who feels like home, it may reflect your early experiences—for better or for worse.
Victimhood often requires agency to overcome; if you feel wronged or overlooked, you’re usually the one who must speak up, initiate repair, or advocate for yourself.
Society often measures a man's success by how useful or dependable he is to others—recognizing this pressure can help you redefine success on your own terms.
Many people search for reassurance from others instead of asking themselves whether they feel good enough; emotional maturity involves being able to have that conversation internally.
Life presents challenges in levels—working through the smaller ones prepares you for the harder, more meaningful ones that come later.
The days feel long, but the years move quickly—awareness of this helps you stay present.
To realize sometimes you can forget the past
entries.author: James Bond - Casino Royale
